explanation: Most piano notes have two or three strings tuned in unison, so its 88 keys need more than 200 strings. An orchestral harp has 47, one for each note.

claims.text: A modern piano has more than 200 strings.
A standard orchestral (concert pedal) harp has 47 strings.
Most notes on a modern piano are strung with two or three strings tuned in unison.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: clean under content:check for writer w-pmusic01w. Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers these music facts (the manifest holds geographic, scientific, Nobel, Olympic and art-collection data), so each high-risk claim needs web evidence from the checkers. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for the harp, an instrument that looks like nothing but strings, which is the trap; a modern grand piano usually has about 220 to 240 strings, so label a states the bounded 'more than 200', which every full-size modern piano exceeds, against the harp's 47. The ratio is far past the 1.1 guard. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: both instruments are familiar worldwide. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: c1 is bounded on purpose, because the exact count varies by maker and model. The labels avoid the wording of the guide's harp encore so that no near-duplicate arises.

claimResults.note: Checker addition x1: role explanation, ref explanation, risk standard. Claim: An orchestral harp has one string for each note, with no strings doubled in unison. issues.note: The explanation's 'An orchestral harp has 47, one for each note' is right as a contrast with the piano's doubled strings, but a harpist may object that pedals let each string sound three pitches. 'one string per note of the scale' would be safer. Recorded as x1.
